items.title: OpenAI ships Codex CLI 0.159.0 — instant interrupt lets you steer the agent mid-response
items.summary: The new opt-in instant_interrupt setting lets you feed new input while Codex is still generating a response or mid-way through a long-running code-mode call, instead of waiting for the turn to finish or killing it outright. The same release compacts the welcome screen, lets you scroll the transcript while deciding on a plan, expands native Mermaid rendering, and adds thread-history pagination for app-server clients.
items.why: The "wait for the whole response or kill it" choice has been the annoying part of every agentic CLI, and this is OpenAI quietly fixing that exact friction point in Codex.
items.action: Upgrade with npm install -g @openai/codex@latest, opt into instant_interrupt, and redirect it mid-task on a real change — then compare how that feels against interrupting Claude Code on the same kind of task.

eval.reason: instant_interrupt is a genuine new capability, plus real workflow fixes — not a rehash or benchmark story.

items.title: CodeGraph: an open-source, pre-indexed code knowledge graph for AI coding agents — 72.6k stars
items.summary: CodeGraph runs a local Rust/tree-sitter parser to build a persisted knowledge graph of your codebase (symbols, calls, imports, inheritance) in SQLite, auto-syncing on file changes via OS-level file watchers. Agents query it through one MCP tool call instead of grepping file-by-file; across 7 real repos (VS Code, Django, Tokio, Excalidraw, OkHttp, Gin, Alamofire) the README reports 88% fewer tool calls, 53% faster, 62% fewer tokens, and 44% cheaper. Fully local, with integrations for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI.
items.why: This is a production-grade, open-source version of almost exactly the semantic-code-graph problem — a graph of a codebase that an agent queries instead of re-deriving context from scratch every time.
items.action: Point it at one of your own repos per the README's quickstart, wire the generated MCP tool into Claude Code or Cursor, and compare how it explores a feature versus its usual grep-and-read pattern.

eval.reason: Substantial tool (Rust parser, SQLite+FTS5, file-watcher sync, MCP server) with a specific 7-repo benchmark.

items.title: Uber's engineering team details MCP Gateway — the platform routing 800+ MCP servers and 5,000+ tools
items.summary: Uber consolidated its fragmented, team-by-team MCP integrations into one gateway: a Registry (control plane) plus Proxy Gateway (data plane) that auto-discovers existing HTTP/gRPC/TChannel APIs via an automated crawler workflow, generates MCP tool schemas with an LLM, and keeps every tool disabled until its owning team explicitly reviews and enables it.
items.why: This is what MCP at scale actually looks like once you're past a handful of hand-wired tools — discovery, token-cost control, and who's allowed to turn a tool on all become real engineering problems.
items.action: If you're exposing any of your own services to agents, skim the post's sections on discovery, token cost, and installation — the same three problems show up fast past a handful of tools.

eval.reason: A real engineering write-up on MCP-at-scale problems (discovery, token cost, governance), not a vendor pitch.

items.title: Stripe's live protocol for AI agents to pay for things, explained with real transaction numbers
items.summary: A write-up from a session with the Stripe and Tempo team walks through MPP (Machine Payments Protocol): a server responds HTTP 402 with payment terms, the agent authorizes via a payment header, and gets a receipt back — no checkout form. It's been live since March 2026 and had roughly 30,000 production transactions by August, used for both micropayment sessions and per-item purchases.
items.why: A working HTTP-level protocol for machine-to-machine payments already processing real transactions, with commenters already debating the hard part: proving who authorized a payment.
items.action: If any side project of yours has an agent doing anything transactional, read the authorization/receipt flow in the linked deep-dive — it's a clean reference for building your own agent-authorization trail, payment or not.

eval.reason: A working, named protocol with real production transaction volume, not a concept pitch.

items.title: Cole Medin: The BEST Jev Use Cases for AI Coding (Absolute Game Changers)
items.summary: Four concrete ways Cole Medin uses the fast, cheap Jev decision-model alongside his coding agent: as a security-hook guard before risky actions, for automated gameplay testing, for real browser-based testing, and to classify incoming GitHub issues and PRs so his workflows pick the right steps and model.
items.why: A working engineer showing exactly where a fast, cheap decision model earns its keep around an LLM coding agent, instead of another hype video.
items.action: 17 minutes — worth it for the security-hooks and workflow-classification segments if you want a concrete pattern for gating or routing your own agent's actions.
